newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Clinton urges media to avoid campaign funds frenzy.
newsitem.headline: Clinton urges media to avoid campaign funds frenzy.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton urged the news media on Wednesday not to rush to judgment on Democratic Party fundraising tactics, saying he had seen no evidence of any wrongdoing.

Clinton, speaking at a news conference on the first full day of a visit to Australia, cautioned against the kind of media frenzy that fed on what ultimately turned out to be false allegations that security guard Richard Jewell was responsible for a bombing at the Atlanta Olympics.

"Remembering what happened to Mr. Jewell in Atlanta, remembering what has happened to so many of the accusations that over the last four years have been made against me and turned out to be totally baseless, i just think that we ought to make sure we (just get) the facts out," he said.

Clinton's comment was prompted by a reporter's suggestion that some White House aides "stonewalled" efforts to get full public disclosure of questionable Democratic fundraising tactics before the November 5 election.
The controversy dogged Clinton in the final days of his re- election campaign, and seems likely to trigger a series of inquiries that could overshadow his second four-year term in the White House.

Critics have focused on the Democratic Party's cultivation of wealthy Asian contributors as it raised the tens of millions of dollars spent to help the president and congressional candidates politically.
Although Clinton has acknowleged that the practice raised questions and had promised to push for campaign finance reform, he has denied any wrongdoing.
"I don't see any problem with any of the information I have seen so far," he said on Wednesday.

The campaign financing controversy gained added momentum on Tuesday with a New York Times report that Bruce Lindsey, a close aide to Clinton, advised other members of the White House not to disclose everything they knew about the matter as news media pressure mounted before the election.

"I don't think there's a real issue here," Clinton said. "One of the things that we have learned the hard way is that when you release something as soon as you have it, somebody is always saying 'Why don't you release something else?"
